examples.title: Bask in it or redirect it
examples.scenario: A reporter wants to profile the boss after a glowing review, and the easy move is to take the credit. Helena Bright, the executive director, knows exactly who built the thing being praised. She recalls how a leader at Eleven Madison Park deflected the spotlight onto the staff who earned it, because a leader who absorbs all the credit starves the team. Minutes before the interview, Helena has to decide whether to bask in the praise herself or redirect it to the people who did the work.
examples.whatToDo: When credit arrives, deflect the spotlight onto the people who actually earned it, because a leader who absorbs all the praise starves the team of the recognition that drives them.

examples.title: Praise from the boss versus outside
examples.scenario: 'My team knows I appreciate them, I tell them all the time,' the manager said. Tobias Frey, her mentor, nodded but pushed. 'Praise from outside lands harder than praise from the boss. At Eleven Madison Park, when reporters called, they were routed to the person who ran the program, like Kirk Kelewae and the beer list.' He slid over a press request. 'Before you answer this, you have to decide which teammate should get this spotlight instead of you.'
examples.whatToDo: Route outside attention, press, and compliments to the person who runs that area, because external recognition lands harder than a boss's praise and turns ordinary staff into recognized specialists.

examples.title: Make her famous or keep her hidden
examples.scenario: Zainab Ali, the practice director, could make her star analyst publicly famous in the field, or keep her quietly indispensable. Fame would make the analyst a target for poaching. Yet hoarding recognition starves people, and the upside in motivation and reputation usually outweighs the loss, a bet leaders at Eleven Madison Park made by elevating their own people. The risk is real. Before the conference speaker list closes, Zainab has to choose between protecting herself from a poach and elevating someone who earned it.
examples.whatToDo: Let your people become celebrated even at the risk of poaching, because the gain in their motivation and your reputation generally outweighs the loss, while hoarding recognition quietly starves them.

examples.title: The team that doubted itself
examples.scenario: Before, Magnus Holt's team doubted its own work and shrank from comparison with bigger names. After a respected industry figure publicly praised them, and Magnus, the studio director, made sure the whole team witnessed it, their sense of their own worth shifted, the way validation from peers like Daniel Boulud once reset how an Eleven Madison Park team saw itself. He kept surfacing outside praise. Twelve months on, the studio carried itself as a peer, not an underdog.
examples.whatToDo: Let the whole team witness respected outsiders validating their work, because validation from people they admire can transform how a team sees its own worth far more than any internal pep talk.

examples.title: The credit she kept
examples.scenario: Turnover of her best people stung, so the division director Reina Castro reviewed the year Monday. Every award and every press mention, she had accepted on the team's behalf and quietly kept the glow. Reading the exit interviews, Reina saw the pattern: by hoarding recognition, she had starved the people who earned it, the opposite of how Eleven Madison Park routed credit to its specialists. The praise had been hers; the talent had walked out the door.
examples.whatToDo: Audit whether you absorb the recognition your team earns, then start redistributing it, because hoarded credit starves the people who did the work and eventually drives them out.

examples.title: Missed deadline, real relationships
examples.scenario: Two weeks before the awards nominations, the founder Desmond Owusu must decide how to handle a missed deadline for an exclusive industry association. He could give up, or lean on real relationships to earn an endorsement anyway, the way Daniel Boulud, Thomas Keller, and Patrick O'Connell vouched for Eleven Madison Park with Relais & Chateaux after it missed the cutoff. He also weighs spotlighting his specialists publicly, since visible credit raises everyone's standard. Desmond chooses between a quiet retreat and a relationship-driven push.
examples.whatToDo: Earn elite endorsement through genuine relationships rather than credentials alone, and make credit visible, because public recognition both opens doors and raises the standard across the whole team.

questions.prompt: A glowing review lands and a reporter wants to feature the boss by name. The team did the work. What does leveraging affirmation suggest the leader do?
choices: Accept the feature personally, since the leader is ultimately responsible and deserves to represent the team's success.
Deflect the spotlight onto the people who earned it, since a leader who absorbs all the credit starves the team.
Decline all press, because attention of any kind tends to make a team complacent and harder to manage.
questions.explanation: A leader who hoards credit starves the team of the recognition that drives them. Deflecting the spotlight onto the people who earned it is the higher-leverage move.

questions.prompt: A manager insists her frequent personal thank-yous are all the recognition her team needs. Engagement is still flat. What is she underrating?
choices: Nothing; praise from a direct boss is the most powerful form of recognition a person can receive.
Her thank-yous are too frequent, so she should praise far less often to make each one count more.
Praise from outside the organization lands harder than a boss's, so routing external recognition to people would do more.
questions.explanation: External validation from respected sources is more powerful than praise handed down from a boss. Channeling outside recognition to the people who earned it does what internal thank-yous cannot.

questions.prompt: When a reporter calls asking about the company's acclaimed coffee program, and the leader knows the junior staffer who actually built it, what should the leader do?
choices: Answer the questions herself, since a polished leader is the safest spokesperson for anything the press asks.
Route the reporter to the staffer who runs the program, turning that person into a recognized specialist in the field.
Decline to comment, because letting a junior person speak to press is too risky for the company's image.
questions.explanation: Routing reporters and compliments to the person who runs a program makes ordinary staff into recognized experts and proves that ownership earns the spotlight, which the leader speaking would erase.

questions.prompt: A leader hesitates to make a talented employee publicly prominent, fearing competitors will poach her. How should you weigh that trade-off?
choices: Elevate her anyway, since the gain in motivation and reputation generally outweighs the poaching risk, while hiding her starves her.
Keep her invisible, since protecting your people from outside attention is usually worth more than any reputational upside.
Promote her only on the condition she signs a long, binding contract, removing the poaching risk for years.
questions.explanation: Letting people become celebrated risks poaching, but the upside in motivation and reputation usually outweighs the loss. Keeping talent invisible to protect it quietly starves the recognition they need.

questions.prompt: When a team that chronically underrates its own work is praised in public by a figure they deeply respect, its whole posture shifts. What does this illustrate?
choices: That praise has no lasting effect, since the team will simply return to doubting itself within a week.
That validation from people you respect lands hardest and witnessing it can transform how a whole team sees its own worth.
That the team was fishing for compliments and the praise mainly fed their egos rather than their work.
questions.explanation: Validation from respected peers lands hardest, and watching it happen can reset a team's sense of its own standing. That shift in self-worth is exactly the leverage affirmation provides.

questions.prompt: A leader accepts every award and press mention on the team's behalf and keeps the glow. Months later his best people leave. How should you assess the connection?
choices: There is no connection, since recognition belongs to whoever leads and talented people leave for unrelated reasons.
The departures prove the people were disloyal, so the leader was right to keep the credit close.
Hoarding recognition starved the people who earned it, so absorbing all the credit helped push the talent out.
questions.explanation: A leader who keeps the credit starves the team of what actually drives them. Hoarding recognition, rather than routing it to the people who earned it, is exactly what drives talent away.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues, 'Making your specialists publicly visible is just vanity that risks losing them.' How should you evaluate that against the idea of public credit?
choices: Agree, since any public recognition mainly feeds egos and exposes you to losing your best people.
Agree, because visible credit rarely changes anything and only invites competitors to come calling.
Push back: public credit inspires others to seek the same recognition and raises the standard across the floor.
questions.explanation: Public credit is not vanity; it inspires other team members to chase the same recognition and lifts the standard for everyone. The motivational and reputational upside is the point.

questions.prompt: You run a team and want recognition to actually drive performance. What is the strongest plan for handling the praise that comes in?
choices: Forward every external compliment, review, and press request straight to the person who earned it, and let them be seen.
Collect all praise centrally and summarize it in your own quarterly update, since one voice keeps the message consistent.
Downplay outside praise, because too much recognition makes a team complacent and lowers its drive.
questions.explanation: Affirmation is a tool only when it is actively redistributed to its rightful source. Passing external praise straight to the people who earned it, and letting them be seen, is what makes it drive performance.

questions.prompt: Your organization just missed a hard cutoff for an elite industry endorsement. You want a path forward that fits how recognition really gets earned. What is the best move?
choices: Lean on genuine relationships with respected peers to vouch for you, since elite endorsement is earned through trust, not deadlines alone.
Accept the rejection quietly, since missing a deadline by any margin means the opportunity is permanently closed.
Publicly attack the association's rules, because the only way past a closed door is to discredit whoever set it.
questions.explanation: Membership and endorsement from elite peers can be earned through relationships, not just credentials or deadlines. Respected figures vouching for you can open a door a missed cutoff seemed to close.

cardFronts.card01: Beyond doing good work, what must a leader decide to do with the credit that arrives?
cardFronts.card02: What does losing your best people right after big praise reveal about who kept the credit?
cardFronts.card03: Why does routing outside praise to the program owner transfer from a restaurant to any team?
cardFronts.card04: What is the most common way leaders let praise stop with the manager?
cardFronts.card05: What one question moves a leader to hand the spotlight to the person who earned it?
cardFronts.card06: Sharing credit sounds generous in theory. What makes a leader actually deflect the spotlight?

coreSkill: Collect the external validation your work earns, glowing reviews, guest notes, peer praise, and channel it to the specific people who earned it. Route reporters and compliments to whoever runs each program, let your people become celebrated even at the risk of poaching, and earn elite endorsement through relationships, because deflected credit drives a team harder than any praise you keep.

ifThenContexts.1: A story about one big external endorsement becomes admired but never redirected.
ifThenContexts.3: Watching respected outsiders praise the team raises everyone's sense of what they can do.
